passage:
Last month I told my whole class about our winter trip to the hills. I said I built a snowman taller than Papa and a yak licked my glove. I was completely sure.
Then Mummy showed me the photos. The snowman came up to my knee. There was no yak. The yak is from my sister Dolma's story; she tells it every time relatives come over. The glove part came from my cousin.
I felt strange, because I can still see the yak in my head, its wet nose and everything.
Now when I tell a story, I say "I think", and sometimes I check the photos first. I'm Sahil, and my memory is a bit of a copycat.

qa.q: How tall was the snowman in the photos?
qa.a: The snowman came up to Sahil's knee.

qa.q: Why was Sahil so sure a yak licked the glove?
qa.a: Hearing Dolma tell the yak story so often made it feel like Sahil's own memory, so Sahil can even see its wet nose.

qa.q: What does Sahil do differently now when telling a story?
qa.a: Sahil says "I think" and sometimes checks the photos first, which leaves room for a memory to be wrong.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel hearing her yak story in Sahil's version?
qa.a: Dolma might be surprised or amused, since it was her story, and may notice how easily family stories get shared.

grounding: It shows a child who retells a family trip with details borrowed from a sister's and a cousin's versions and fully believes them.

passage:
Class 5 teacher's note, after the "My Holiday" talks
Chaitanya described the family trip to the salt desert in detail: flamingos, a camel that sat on the car, getting lost at night. Chaitanya's older brothers were in my class in earlier years and gave nearly the same talk, camel included.
When I asked, Chaitanya said firmly, "I remember it, sir. I was there." I believe Chaitanya means it; there was no sign of making things up. Chaitanya's mother later told me the camel story is the eldest brother's favourite, told at every family dinner.
I didn't mark it wrong. Next week, the class will draw one thing they remember from a trip and then check it with a photo or a family member, just to see what changes.
Lalit

qa.q: What did Chaitanya say about the camel when asked?
qa.a: Chaitanya said firmly, "I remember it, sir. I was there."

qa.q: Why is Chaitanya so sure the camel sat on the car?
qa.a: Chaitanya feels confident and sincere, because the camel story told at every family dinner has become part of Chaitanya's own memory and feels completely real.

qa.q: What activity did Lalit plan, and why is it a kind approach?
qa.a: The class will draw a trip memory and check it against a photo or a family member, which shows memories change without accusing anyone of lying.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya's older brothers react to hearing their camel story from Chaitanya?
qa.a: They might laugh or feel proud that their story is so memorable, or insist Chaitanya was too small to remember it.

grounding: It shows a child who retells a family trip using older brothers' versions and sincerely believes every detail.

passage:
Sunday
Diary, today Ammi said I have "Salma Apa's memory". Here's why.
At dinner I told Khalu about our trip to the lake when I was six. I said the boat nearly tipped over and a duck stole my biscuit. Salma Apa said, "Kiran, that was ME. You were asleep in the car." Ammi laughed and agreed!
But I REMEMBER it. I can see the duck's orange feet.
Then Apa said she has told that story so often that I must have heard it a hundred times. Maybe my brain just put me in it?
It's a bit creepy but also funny. Tomorrow I'm going to ask Abbu what he remembers and write it down before anyone else talks.
Kiran

qa.q: What did Kiran say the duck stole?
qa.a: Kiran said a duck stole the biscuit.

qa.q: Why does Kiran still feel sure about the duck?
qa.a: Kiran feels certain and a bit puzzled, because Kiran can picture the duck's orange feet, and hearing Salma Apa's story so often makes it feel like Kiran's own memory.

qa.q: What does Kiran plan to do tomorrow, and why is it a smart check?
qa.a: Kiran will ask Abbu what he remembers and write it down before anyone else talks, so no other version gets mixed in.

qa.q: How might Salma Apa feel when Kiran tells her story as Kiran's own?
qa.a: Salma may feel amused but a little protective of her memory, since she was the one near the duck while Kiran was asleep.

grounding: It shows a child who retells a family trip with parts taken from an older sister's version and believes them fully.

passage: In the village school near Champhai, Shalini Ma'am asked each child to tell the class about a trip. Lalremsiami, ten, stood up with shining eyes. "We went to the waterfall with my whole family. My uncle's jeep got stuck in the mud and we all pushed. I slipped and fell into the stream, and a big fish swam right past my leg. Then it rained so hard we slept in the jeep." The class gasped. That evening her two older brothers laughed. "Siami, you didn't fall in the stream," said Zela. "I did." "And the fish was my story from last year," said Mapuia. Lalremsiami stared at them. "No, I remember. I remember the cold water." Her mother said gently, "You were asleep in the jeep when Zela fell in." Lalremsiami went quiet, still sure she could feel the water.

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami's family go on the trip?
qa.a: To the waterfall.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel when her brothers said the stream and the fish weren't hers?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt confused and went quiet, still sure she could feel the cold water, because hearing her brothers' stories had become part of her own memory.

qa.q: How could Lalremsiami's mother help without making her feel foolish?
qa.a: She could look at trip photos with her and sort out together which parts were Siami's own and which came from her brothers, treating it as a normal puzzle of memory.

qa.q: How might Zela feel hearing his own fall told as someone else's?
qa.a: He might feel amused but also a little annoyed, as if his own adventure had been borrowed.

grounding: A girl retells a family trip with parts taken from her brothers' stories and believes them fully, showing memory is rebuilt each time.

passage: At dinner in their house outside Gothenburg, Lars, nine, told his grandmother about the summer trip to the islands. "The ferry was huge, and a seal jumped right onto the deck, and the captain let me steer." Grandma clapped. His older brother Daniel put down his fork. "Lars, the seal was on a rock, far away. I'm the one who said it looked like it wanted to jump. And the captain let me hold the wheel, not you. You were eating ice cream." Lars went red. "No, I remember. The wheel was cold." Their father scrolled to a photo on his phone: Daniel at the wheel, Lars behind him with a cone. Lars looked at it for a long time. "But I remember it," he said quietly.

qa.q: Where was the seal really, according to Daniel?
qa.a: The seal was on a rock, far away.

qa.q: Why does Lars say quietly "But I remember it" even after seeing the photo?
qa.a: His memory has been rebuilt from Daniel's version, so it feels fully real, and seeing proof otherwise leaves him confused and a bit embarrassed.

qa.q: What could the family do to help Lars without making him feel he lied?
qa.a: They could explain that everyone's memories change when they hear others' stories, and enjoy sorting out the photos together.

qa.q: How does Daniel feel about Lars's version?
qa.a: Daniel seems a little annoyed that his turn at the wheel was taken over, and wants his own part of the trip recognised.

grounding: A boy retells a family trip with his brother's details as his own and believes them, showing that memory is rebuilt rather than replayed.
